items.title: Q1 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · Ben Jonson
items.stem: A classical influence on Ben Jonson's Volpone is

structured.lead: A classical influence on Ben Jonson's Volpone is
structured.options_hint: Juvenal Aristophanes Plautus Terence

items.explanation: Ben Jonson's comedy Volpone (1606) draws heavily on the classical Greek Old Comedy of Aristophanes (as well as Roman satirists like Juvenal and Lucian) in its beast-fable caricatures, biting topical satire, and dark, un-romantic comic resolution.

items.title: Q2 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit II: Poetry · Rudyard Kipling
items.stem: Kipling's "The White Man's Burden" is addressed to

structured.lead: Kipling's "The White Man's Burden" is addressed to
structured.options_hint: The American imperial mission in the Phi

options: The American imperial mission in the Philippines
The Belgian colonial expansion in the Congo
The British Imperial presence in Nigeria
The British colonial entry into Afghanistan
items.explanation: Published in February 1899 with the subtitle 'The United States and the Philippine Islands,' Rudyard Kipling's poem 'The White Man's Burden' was directly addressed to the United States to urge American imperial annexation of the Philippines after the Spanish-American War.

items.explanation: Harriet Monroe founded Poetry: A Magazine of Verse in Chicago in October 1912, publishing landmark modernist poems such as T. S. Eliot's 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock' and Ezra Pound's Imagist verse.

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit II: Poetry · Geoffrey Chaucer
items.stem: Who among the following was Geoffrey Chaucer's contemporary ?

structured.lead: Who among the following was Geoffrey Chaucer's contemporary ?
structured.options_hint: Thomas Chatterton John Gower Thomas Shad

items.explanation: Fourteenth-century poet John Gower (c. 1330–1408), author of Confessio Amantis, was a close personal friend and contemporary of Geoffrey Chaucer, who dedicated Troilus and Criseyde to 'moral Gower.'

items.title: Q5 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT written by Walter Scott ?

structured.lead: Which of the following is NOT written by Walter Scott ?
structured.options_hint: Ivanhoe Lady of the Lake Heart of Midlot

items.explanation: Ivanhoe (1819), The Lady of the Lake (1810), and The Heart of Midlothian (1818) are celebrated works by Sir Walter Scott, whereas 'The English Mail-Coach' (1849) is a famous visionary prose essay by Thomas De Quincey.

items.title: Q6 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Edward Said
items.stem: "Provincializing Europe" is a concept propounded by

structured.lead: "Provincializing Europe" is a concept propounded by
structured.options_hint: Edward Said Paul Gilroy Abdul R. Gurnah

items.explanation: Postcolonial historian and Subaltern Studies theorist Dipesh Chakrabarty propounded the concept in his landmark book Provincializing Europe: Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference (2000), critiquing the treatment of European history as the universal norm of modernity.

items.title: Q7 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · unit-4-non-fictional-prose · Mary Wollstonecraft
items.stem: The earliest tract on feminism is

structured.lead: The earliest tract on feminism is
structured.options_hint: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex Virg

options: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex
Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own
Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
Mary Astell's A Serious Proposal to the Ladies
items.explanation: Published in 1694—nearly a century before Mary Wollstonecraft's 1792 Vindication—Mary Astell's A Serious Proposal to the Ladies, for the Advancement of their True and Greatest Interest is the earliest feminist tract on the list, earning Astell the title 'the first English feminist.'

items.title: Q9 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)

items.stem: Which Chaucerian text parodies Dante's The Divine Comedy ?

structured.lead: Which Chaucerian text parodies Dante's The Divine Comedy ?
structured.options_hint: The Canterbury Tales The Book of the Duc

items.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer's dream-vision poem The House of Fame (c. 1379–1380) comically parodies Dante's The Divine Comedy, featuring a pedantic, talkative golden eagle (echoing Purgatorio IX and Virgil) who carries the terrified poet 'Geffrey' into the heavens.

options: The Ballad of the Reading Gaol
items.explanation: Written in 1913–1914 and published posthumously in 1971, E. M. Forster's novel Maurice is a classic work of homosexual fiction depicting the same-sex love and eventual happiness of Maurice Hall and Alec Scudder in Edwardian England.

items.title: Q12 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit II: Poetry · W. B. Yeats
items.stem: W.B. Yeats's "Easter 1916" is

structured.lead: W.B. Yeats's "Easter 1916" is
structured.options_hint: a response to a major political uprising

options: a response to a major political uprising
a reminiscence of his visit to a nursery school
a love poem for Maud Gonne
an ode to his native country
items.explanation: W. B. Yeats's poem 'Easter, 1916' is a profound elegiac meditation on the Easter Rising of April 1916 in Dublin, in which Irish Republicans staged an armed insurrection against British rule, declaring that 'A terrible beauty is born.'

items.title: Q13 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: William Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity is

structured.lead: William Empson's Seven Types of Ambiguity is
structured.options_hint: A structuralist study of narrative A pie

items.explanation: William Empson's landmark critical study Seven Types of Ambiguity (1930), written while studying under I. A. Richards at Cambridge, is a close-reading analysis of poetic ambivalence and the multiple layers of verbal meaning in English verse.

items.title: Q14 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Kingsley
items.stem: Who among the following is associated with the ideology of Utilitarianism ?

structured.lead: Who among the following is associated with the ideology of Utilitarianism ?
structured.options_hint: Froude Charles Kingsley Mill Cardinal Ne

items.explanation: Nineteenth-century British philosopher and political economist John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) was the foremost exponent of Utilitarianism—the ethical doctrine of 'the greatest happiness of the greatest number' founded by Jeremy Bentham—which Mill refined in his treatise Utilitarianism (1861).

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The 'Condition of England' literature refers to

structured.lead: The 'Condition of England' literature refers to
structured.options_hint: The literature written by the labour cla

options: The literature written by the labour class
The literature of England extolling living conditions
The literature of England depicting the vulnerability of labour classes
The literature of England depicting the imperial projects abroad
items.explanation: Named after a phrase coined by Thomas Carlyle in Chartism (1839), 'Condition-of-England' literature refers to 1840s and 1850s Victorian social-problem novels—by Dickens, Disraeli, Gaskell, and Kingsley—depicting industrial poverty and the vulnerability of the working classes.

items.title: Q16 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Philip Sidney
items.stem: Philip Sidney wrote An Apology for Poetry in immediate response to

structured.lead: Philip Sidney wrote An Apology for Poetry in immediate response to
structured.options_hint: Plato's Republic Aristotle's Poetics Ste

options: Stephen Gosson's The School of Abuse
Jeremy Collier's Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage
items.explanation: Sir Philip Sidney wrote An Apology for Poetry (also published as The Defence of Poesie, composed c. 1580, published 1595) in immediate response to Stephen Gosson's Puritan invective against poetry and theatre, The Schoole of Abuse (1579), which Gosson had unauthorizedly dedicated to Sidney.

items.title: Q17 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism

items.title: Q20 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)

structured.options_hint: Epicureanism Humanism Stoicism Cynicism

items.explanation: Samuel Johnson's poem 'The Vanity of Human Wishes' (1749), an imitation of Juvenal's Tenth Satire, expresses a profound Christian Stoicism, surveying the futility of worldly ambition and counselling patience, fortitude, and submission to divine will.

items.explanation: The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations (published posthumously in 1633) is the celebrated collection of metaphysical devotional lyrics by Anglican priest and poet George Herbert, including 'The Altar,' 'Easter Wings,' and 'The Collar.'

items.title: Q24 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · Ben Jonson
items.stem: Ben Jonson's comedies are

structured.lead: Ben Jonson's comedies are
structured.options_hint: Volpone, Bartholomew Fair, The Shoemaker

options: Volpone, Bartholomew Fair, The Shoemaker's Holiday
Volpone, The Alchemist, The Knight of the Burning Pestle
items.explanation: Volpone (1606), Epicoene, or the Silent Woman (1609), and The Alchemist (1610) are three of Ben Jonson's greatest Jacobean city comedies. By contrast, The Shoemaker's Holiday was written by Thomas Dekker and The Knight of the Burning Pestle by Francis Beaumont.

structured.lead: Given below are two statements:

statements.label: Assertion (A)
statements.text: Dr Johnson's The Lives of the Poets carries critical and biographical studies of poets he admired. It does not, however, carry a life of William Wordsworth.

statements.label: Reason (R)
statements.text: Dr. Johnson singled out poets whom he not only admired but also adored. This explains his omission of Wordsworth

structured.options_hint: (A) is wrong but (R) is correct. (A) is

items.explanation: Dr. Samuel Johnson's Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets (1779–1781) indeed omits William Wordsworth (who was a child when it appeared and published his first poems in 1793, nine years after Johnson's death in 1784), whereas Reason (R) is completely false because the 52 poets were chosen by London booksellers rather than adored by Johnson.

structured.lead:
"How can what an Englishman believes be heresy ? It is a contradiction in terms."
This means
1. An Englishman does not know what heresy is.
2. An Englishman has no beliefs.
3. And, therefore, there is no question of his heresy.
4. And, therefore, there cannot be any question of his acting his beliefs.
structured.options_hint: 1 and 4 are correct 2 and 1 are correct

items.explanation: Based on the satirical remark on English insularity from George Bernard Shaw's Saint Joan ('How can what an Englishman believes be heresy? It is a contradiction in terms'), the logical deductions are that an Englishman does not recognize what heresy is (1) and therefore there is no question of his heresy (3).

structured.lead: Which of the following is an essentially Freudian concept ?
structured.options_hint: Archetype The Uncanny The Absurd The Ima

items.explanation: 'The Uncanny' (Das Unheimliche) is an essentially Freudian psychoanalytic concept elaborated by Sigmund Freud in his famous 1919 essay on the eerie familiarity of repressed material. ('Archetype' is Jungian, 'The Absurd' is Existentialist, and 'The Imaginary' is Lacanian.)

items.title: Q46 · Dec 2009 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies
items.stem:
Read the following passage carefully, and select the right answers from the alternatives given below in the question 46 to 50 :

It would be more accurate to say that discourse, rather than language, plays a crucial part in structuring our experience. The whole idea of 'language' is something of a fiction : what we normally refer to as 'language' can more realistically be seen as heterogeneous collection of discourses. Each of us has access to a range of discourses, and it is these different discourses which give us access to, or enable us to perform, different 'selves'. A discourse can be conceptualized as a 'system of statements which cohere around common meanings and values'. So, for example, in contemporary Britain there are discourses which can be labelled 'conservative' – that is, discourses which emphasize values and meanings where the status quo is cherished : and there are discourses which can be labelled 'patriarchal' – that is, discourses which emphasize meanings and values which assume the superiority of males. Dominant discourses such as these appear 'natural' : they are powerful precisely because they are able to make invisible the fact that they are just one among many different discourses.

Theorizing language in this way is still new in linguistics (to the extent that many linguists would not regard analysis in terms of discourses as being part of linguistics). One of the advantages of talking about discourses rather than about language is that the concept 'discourse' acknowledges the value-laden nature of language. There is no neutral discourse : whenever we speak we have to choose between different systems of meaning, different sets of values. This process allows us to show how language is implicated in our construction of different 'selves' : different discourses position us in different ways in relation to the world.
